findings.summary: Page 1 shows code and results before the idea in places, and the deduction failure is stated as bare lines rather than a clear contrast.
findings.evidence:
max(1, 2) deduces T = int
max(1, 2.5) fails: T conflicts, so give T explicitly
cpp
template<typename T>
T max(T a, T b)
findings.fix: State the one-line idea first ('T is deduced from the arguments; conflicting arguments fail'), then show the code, and present the deduction cases as a small table (call | T | result).

findings.summary: The Class Templates table is malformed: the header row has an empty first cell, and the specialization and function-template rules sit as loose lines under it, so it is unclear whether they belong to the table.
findings.fix: Keep the table to the two class-args rows and move specialization into its own bullets: 'Full specialization: template<> struct S<int>{} replaces the template for one type'. Add a code example for the specialization.

findings.summary: The 'Common Mistakes' bullets give a symptom or a fix but not both, so the pairing is unclear.
findings.evidence:
Definitions not in the header: linker reports undefined reference
Dependent name without typename: write typename T::value_type
findings.fix: Write each as a mistake | symptom | fix table row. State why template definitions must be in the header, since the compiler needs them at the point of instantiation.

findings.summary: The vector<bool> note is a one-sentence dump that holds the cause and two fixes. It also sits under the Range-for table without a heading.
findings.evidence:
vector<bool>
auto& fails on vector<bool>: its proxy is a temporary. Use auto&& or const auto&.
findings.fix: Split into two bullets (cause, fix) and add it as a row in the Range-for table, or put it under a 'Pitfall' label.

findings.summary: The decltype(auto) code example comes after only a brief rule, and the dangling-reference lesson is only a code comment.
findings.fix: Add a bullet before the code: 'decltype(auto) with return (y) returns int& to a local, which dangles', so the pitfall is stated in prose, not only in a comment.

findings.summary: The Interview Point section repeats the structured binding and constexpr vs const content from earlier on the page and in Mistakes, and its question-and-answer lines are packed into single lines.
findings.evidence:
constexpr vs const? const can be set at run time
...
constexpr is not const: const may be initialized at run time
findings.fix: Drop the duplicate, or reduce the interview section to a Q | A table. Keep the constexpr vs const explanation in one place.

findings.summary: The constexpr function row says 'compile time or run time' without saying when each applies, and the constinit row does not say what constinit is for.
findings.evidence:
constexpr function | compile time or run time
constinit (C++20) | static initialization, still mutable
findings.fix: Say that a constexpr function runs at compile time only when its arguments are constant expressions or its result is used in a constant context, and that constinit prevents the static initialization order problem.

findings.summary: The `overloaded` helper in the `visit` example is used without being defined or explained, so the example does not compile as shown.
findings.fix: Add the two-line definition `template<class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; }; template<class... Ts> overloaded(Ts...) -> overloaded<Ts...>;`. Or note that `overloaded` is a user-written helper, not part of std.

findings.summary: The variant code example is shown before the idea behind visit is stated, and the one-line explanation of visit comes after the code.
findings.fix: Put 'visit dispatches on the active type; the overloaded helper supplies one lambda per alternative' before the code. Note that overloaded is a user-defined helper, not part of std.

findings.summary: The 'Default variant' note is a prose paragraph, and it follows the decision table without a clear link to it.
findings.evidence:
Default variant
It holds its first type. If that is not default-constructible, put std::monostate first.
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: 'Default-constructed variant holds its first alternative' and 'If the first type is not default-constructible, put std::monostate first'.

findings.summary: The requires-expression bullet crams a long inline syntax string into one line, and the 'three ways to apply Number' caption sits after the code without a clear anchor.
findings.evidence:
A requires expression checks syntax: requires(T a) { a + a; { a.size() } -> std::convertible_to<size_t>; }
three ways to apply Number
findings.fix: Move the requires expression into its own code block with a one-line idea before it, and label each of the three forms in the code with a comment.

findings.summary: The 'Remember' summary repeats the table and calls C++11 the big break while the table also lists large C++20 additions, so the cheat sheet gives the learner two ways to rank the standards.
findings.evidence: C++11 is the big break (move semantics, smart pointers); C++20 adds concepts to constrain templates.
findings.fix: Keep it to one bullet per standard, or remove it. The table already carries the content.
